content: A systematic review of nine original studies was conducted to critically evaluate and summarize the current evidence on the cost-benefit and cost-effectiveness of screening and treating latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI). The outcomes assessed included the incremental cost per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) or life year (LY) gained, as well as the incremental cost per tuberculosis (TB) case averted. Providing preventive therapy without LTBI screening for individuals with HIV was found to be cost-effective or cost-saving compared to no treatment in both resource-limited settings (e.g., Uganda, India, Zambia) and high-income countries (e.g., Italy). However, this strategy was not cost-effective for other populations, such as contacts of active TB cases or patients with systemic lupus erythematosus. In high TB incidence settings, a study suggested that screening without testing for LTBI was the most cost-effective approach for children aged 0–2 years and the preferred strategy for children aged 3–5 years who were household contacts of TB cases. The cost-effectiveness of interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) compared to tuberculin skin tests (TSTs) was influenced by the relative diagnostic performance of the tests. Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination reduced the specificity of TST, favoring IGRA-based strategies. Two-step strategies (IGRA following TST) were the most cost-effective in high-income countries and high-risk populations. In contrast, TST-only strategies were favorable in two U.S. studies: one assumed low treatment completion rates, and the other involved a low-risk population (U.S. military recruits), where all screening strategies were not cost-effective. In 13 studies that expressed costs in U.S. dollars, the cost of ruling out active TB in individuals eligible for LTBI preventive treatment (including chest radiographs, clinical evaluations, and liver function tests) ranged from $28 to $188. Most of these studies were conducted in high-income and upper-middle-income countries, with one exception in India. Regarding diagnostic strategies, either TST or IGRA can be used to test for LTBI. However, IGRA should not replace TST in lowand middle-income countries due to cost considerations and limited evidence quality. For ruling out active TB, individuals should be assessed for TB symptoms and undergo chest radiography before initiating LTBI treatment. Those with TB symptoms should undergo further investigation for active TB and other conditions. The accuracy of chest X-rays (CXR) in ruling out active TB among LTBI treatment candidates was evaluated in studies from high TB burden countries. Limitations included selection bias, low reference standard use, and indirectness of study populations. Similarly, the accuracy of TB symptom screening was assessed, but the studies had significant limitations, including imprecise estimates and high variability in study populations. For LTBI treatment, several regimens have demonstrated efficacy in preventing progression to active TB. Isoniazid (INH) administered daily for six months has been a longstanding treatment. Other regimens include daily rifampicin (RMP) for 3–4 months, daily INH and RMP for three months, and weekly INH and rifapentine (RPT) for 12 weeks. Safety concerns, particularly hepatotoxicity, are critical in LTBI treatment, as most treated individuals are healthy. Pyrazinamide-containing regimens were excluded from further analysis due to severe hepatotoxicity risks. A systematic review on drug resistance found no significant increase in isoniazid resistance with 6–12 months of INH treatment. Similarly, rifamycin-containing regimens did not significantly increase rifamycin resistance. However, evidence quality was low to very low, and further research is needed to confirm these findings. In terms of cost-effectiveness, shorter regimens (e.g., 3–4 months of RMP) were associated with lower liver-related adverse events compared to six months of INH. Mixed treatment comparisons suggested that no single regimen was consistently superior across all outcomes. The choice of LTBI treatment regimen should consider efficacy, safety, cost, feasibility, and the risk of fostering drug resistance.
